competencies.label: Leadership
competencies.blurb: Whether you set direction, mobilized people without relying on title, and owned the outcome.

competencies.label: Teamwork & Inclusion
competencies.blurb: How you build on others' ideas, bring quieter or different voices in, and make the whole team better.

competencies.label: Impact & Drive
competencies.blurb: Whether you set ambitious goals and kept pushing through obstacles to deliver measurable results.

competencies.label: Overcoming a Challenge
competencies.blurb: How you respond when things go wrong: composure, adaptability, and persistence under pressure.

competencies.label: Failure & Learning
competencies.blurb: Whether you own mistakes honestly, extract real lessons, and show changed behavior afterward.

competencies.label: Conflict & Difficult People
competencies.blurb: How you handle disagreement with empathy and directness while preserving the relationship and the goal.

competencies.label: Persuasion & Influence
competencies.blurb: How you changed someone's mind or a group's direction, especially without formal authority.

competencies.label: Analytical Problem Solving
competencies.blurb: How you broke down an ambiguous problem, used data and judgment, and reached a sound recommendation.

competencies.label: Ethics & Integrity
competencies.blurb: Whether you do the right thing when it is costly, uncomfortable, or unobserved.

competencies.label: Entrepreneurial Initiative
competencies.blurb: Whether you spot opportunities no one asked you to pursue and build something from nothing.

firm_frameworks.name: Personal Experience Interview (PEI)
firm_frameworks.note: Each interview typically goes deep on one story tied to one dimension, with the interviewer probing your specific actions, reasoning and others' reactions for 10-15 minutes. McKinsey advises preparing two examples per dimension and focusing on your specific role and key actions.

firm_frameworks.name: Behavioral / fit questions within case interviews
firm_frameworks.note: BCG says it reviews responses against its values and core competencies; behavioral questions usually open or close case interviews and explore your experience, skills and motivation for joining BCG. Relate answers back to the job.

firm_frameworks.name: Experience / behavioral interview
dimensions: Fit with Bain's operating principles and the role
firm_frameworks.note: Bain describes behavioral questions as a conversational chat with future colleagues, sometimes a dedicated interview and sometimes woven into case rounds; no fixed named dimensions are published, so expect broad fit, team orientation and 'why Bain' probing.

questions.q: Tell me about yourself.
follow_ups: What thread connects your career moves?
Which experience are you proudest of?
What would your last manager say about you?
questions.tip: Keep it to 90 seconds: past, pivot, present, and why you are in this room.

questions.q: Walk me through your resume, focusing on the decisions you made.
follow_ups: Why did you leave that role when you did?
What did you learn there that you could not have learned elsewhere?
What would you do differently?
questions.tip: Narrate choices, not job descriptions; each transition should have a clear 'why'.

questions.q: Why consulting, and why now?
follow_ups: What else are you considering?
What do you think you will dislike about the job?
How do you know consulting fits your working style?
questions.tip: Anchor in something concrete from your past work, not generic 'learning curve' language.

questions.q: Why this firm rather than its peers?
follow_ups: Who have you spoken with here?
What surprised you in those conversations?
If you got offers from all three, how would you decide?
questions.tip: Cite specific people and specific moments; generic culture claims sound interchangeable.

questions.q: Why did you decide to pursue an MBA, and why at this point in your career?
follow_ups: What gap were you trying to close?
What have you done so far to close it?
What would you have done without the MBA?
questions.tip: Show a deliberate decision, then link it to the consulting goal.

questions.q: What are your greatest strengths? Give me evidence for one.
follow_ups: How would a peer describe that strength?
When has that strength backfired?
How will it show up on a client team?
questions.tip: Name two or three, then prove one with a quick story.

questions.q: What is a genuine development area for you, and what are you doing about it?
follow_ups: When did it last cost you something?
How do you measure progress?
What feedback prompted you to notice it?
questions.tip: Pick a real, non-disqualifying weakness and show active, recent steps to fix it.

questions.q: Why are you interested in product or tech roles?
follow_ups: What product do you admire and why?
How would you improve it?
Why not stay in consulting long term?
questions.tip: Tie interest to a product you actually built or shipped, and show user empathy.

questions.q: Tell me about a product or feature you took from idea to launch.
follow_ups: How did you decide what to cut from scope?
What metric told you it worked?
What did engineering push back on?
questions.tip: Separate what you decided from what the team built; quantify adoption or impact.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to change a group's direction.
follow_ups: How did you know the group was on the wrong path?
Who resisted most and why?
What did you say in the key conversation?
questions.tip: PEI-style: expect the interviewer to zoom in on one conversation, so remember specifics.

questions.q: Describe a time you led a team where you had no formal authority.
follow_ups: How did you get people to commit?
What happened when someone did not deliver?
What would the team say about your role?
questions.tip: Emphasize how you earned buy-in, not the title you lacked.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you developed someone else's capabilities.
follow_ups: How did you diagnose what they needed?
What feedback did you give that was hard to hear?
Where are they now?
questions.tip: Show patience and specific coaching actions, and the person's outcome.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to take charge when things were falling apart.
follow_ups: What did you do in the first hour?
What did you delegate and why?
How did you keep people calm?
questions.tip: Show structure under pressure: triage, clear roles, communication.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you brought out the best in a diverse team.
follow_ups: How did you notice someone was not contributing?
What did you change in how the team worked?
What was the result?
questions.tip: McKinsey frames this as inclusive leadership; show concrete actions that drew in different voices.

questions.q: Describe working with a teammate who was not pulling their weight.
follow_ups: What did you assume at first and were you right?
How did you raise it?
How did the relationship end up?
questions.tip: Seek to understand before judging; avoid blaming the teammate.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you put the team's success ahead of your own.
follow_ups: What did it cost you?
Did anyone notice?
Would you do it again?
questions.tip: Make the trade-off real and the team outcome specific.

questions.q: Tell me about a time a teammate's perspective changed your approach.
follow_ups: Why did you initially disagree?
What convinced you?
How did you give them credit?
questions.tip: Shows openness; name what you changed specifically.

questions.q: Tell me about your most significant accomplishment.
follow_ups: Why was it hard?
What would have happened without you?
How do you know it mattered?
questions.tip: Pick the story with the clearest personal impact, not the biggest team result.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you set a goal others thought was unrealistic.
follow_ups: Why did you set it that high?
When did you nearly give up?
What did you hit versus plan?
questions.tip: Quantify the gap between baseline, target and outcome.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you made a significant impact on an organization.
follow_ups: How did you measure it?
Who else could claim credit?
Is the change still in place?
questions.tip: Personal impact dimension: be explicit about what you, not we, did.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you faced a major setback. How did you respond?
follow_ups: How did you feel in the moment?
What was your first move?
What support did you seek?
questions.tip: Show emotional honesty plus a concrete recovery plan.

questions.q: Describe a time you had to deliver with very little information or guidance.
follow_ups: How did you decide where to start?
What assumptions did you make?
How did you validate them?
questions.tip: Show a structured approach to ambiguity, mirroring how you work on a case.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you juggled competing high-stakes priorities.
follow_ups: How did you prioritize?
What did you drop and who did you tell?
What would you do differently?
questions.tip: Name the explicit prioritization logic and how you communicated trade-offs.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you failed.
follow_ups: What was your specific role in the failure?
What did you do right after?
Where have you applied the lesson since?
questions.tip: Pick a real failure you caused; the reflection and later application matter most.

questions.q: Tell me about the toughest feedback you have received.
follow_ups: Did you agree at first?
What did you change?
How did the person see you afterward?
questions.tip: Show you took it seriously and changed observable behavior.

questions.q: Describe a decision you made that turned out to be wrong.
follow_ups: What information did you have at the time?
Was it a bad decision or a bad outcome?
How do you decide differently now?
questions.tip: Distinguish decision quality from outcome; show updated judgment.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager or a senior stakeholder.
follow_ups: How did you raise it?
What did you do when they did not agree?
What was the outcome?
questions.tip: Show respectful directness and willingness to commit once a decision is made.

questions.q: Describe a time you dealt with a difficult client or customer.
follow_ups: What was really driving their behavior?
What did you concede and what did you hold firm on?
How did the relationship end up?
questions.tip: Diagnose the underlying interest; consulting interviewers love this for client readiness.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict between two other people.
follow_ups: How did you get involved?
What did each side want?
How did you stay neutral?
questions.tip: Show facilitation: separating positions from interests.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you persuaded a skeptical audience.
follow_ups: What was their main objection?
How did you tailor your argument?
What did you do when data was not enough?
questions.tip: Show you adapted to the audience, not just repeated your case louder.

questions.q: Describe a time you convinced someone much more senior to change course.
follow_ups: How did you get time with them?
What was the pivotal moment?
What was the risk to you?
questions.tip: Courageous change: show you took a personal risk and managed it smartly.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you drove change people resisted.
follow_ups: Why did people resist?
Who did you win over first?
How did you make it stick?
questions.tip: Maps to McKinsey's courageous change; show a sequence of actions over time.

questions.q: Tell me about the most complex problem you have solved.
follow_ups: How did you structure it?
What data was missing and how did you handle that?
How did you communicate the answer?
questions.tip: Walk through your structure explicitly; this is a mini-case in story form.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to make a decision quickly with incomplete data.
follow_ups: What was the cost of waiting?
What did you do to limit downside?
How did it turn out?
questions.tip: Show judgment and risk mitigation, not recklessness.

questions.q: Tell me about an insight you found that others had missed.
follow_ups: How did you spot it?
Why had others missed it?
What action did it lead to?
questions.tip: Tie the insight to a concrete business decision and outcome.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you were pressured to do something you felt was wrong.
follow_ups: Who applied the pressure?
What did you say?
What were the consequences for you?
questions.tip: Show calm firmness and a clear escalation path; a story from a controls, audit or compliance setting works well.

questions.q: Describe a time you had to deliver bad news or admit an error to a client or manager.
follow_ups: Why not just fix it quietly?
How did they react?
What happened to trust afterward?
questions.tip: Show you surfaced it early and came with a fix.

questions.q: Tell me about a time the right thing to do was not clear-cut.
follow_ups: What options did you consider?
Who did you consult?
Would you decide the same today?
questions.tip: Show a principled reasoning process rather than a tidy answer.

questions.q: Tell me about something you started from scratch.
follow_ups: Why did no one do it before?
How did you get resources?
What happened after you left?
questions.tip: Entrepreneurial drive: stress that you spotted the gap unprompted and owned it end to end.

questions.q: Describe a time you went well beyond your job description.
follow_ups: Why did you take it on?
What did you deprioritize?
How was it recognized?
questions.tip: Show judgment about when stepping beyond scope was worth it.

star_guide: Situation and task in 20-30 seconds: just enough context (who, what, stakes) for the interviewer to follow.
Spend about 60% of the time on your actions: say 'I', name specific steps, conversations and decisions, and why you chose them.
Surface the obstacle or tension early so the story has stakes; interviewers remember conflict and turning points.
Quantify the result (%, $, time, people) and say what would have happened without you.
Close with a one-line reflection: what you learned and how you have applied it since.
Aim for about 2 minutes on the first pass, then let the interviewer steer; PEI follow-ups can go 10-15 minutes deep on one story.
Prepare 8-10 flexible stories mapped across competencies, with at least two per McKinsey PEI dimension, and keep details (names, numbers, dialogue) memorable but not scripted.
